name: Chota
significance: De facto capital ~1740s–1788; "City of Peace"; home of Attakullakulla, Oconostota, and Nancy Ward (Nan'yehi)
status: Mostly submerged under Tellico Lake; monument marks the site

name: Tanasi
significance: Capital ~1721–1730; namesake of the state of Tennessee

name: Great Tellico
significance: Capital under Moytoy ~1730; Tahlequah, OK likely named for it

name: Citico
significance: Largest warrior contingent per Lt. Henry Timberlake's 1761 visit
status: Submerged; National Register of Historic Places listed

name: Tuskegee
significance: Birthplace of Sequoyah, creator of the Cherokee syllabary

name: Chilhowee
significance: Home of Old Abraham; Old Tassel murdered here in 1788 under a flag of truce

name: Tomotley
significance: Peace town; residence of Attakullakulla

name: Toqua
significance: Major archaeological site with mound complex

name: Nikwasi (Noquisiyi)
significance: Mother town; ~1,000-year-old platform mound; home of the Nunne'hi (immortal spirit people). Deed returned to EBCI on February 26, 2026.
status: Mound survives in Franklin, NC; ownership returned to EBCI in 2026

name: Cowee
significance: Capital of Middle Towns by William Bartram's era (1770s)

name: Etchoe
significance: 1760 battle site during the Anglo-Cherokee War

name: Keowee
significance: Largest Lower Town; main trading path to British colonial settlements at Charleston. Permanently destroyed in 1776 by Major Andrew Williamson's SC militia. Never reoccupied.

name: Estatoe
significance: Lower Town burned 1760 by Montgomery, resettled by 1762. Permanently destroyed 1776 by Williamson. Never reoccupied.

name: Tugaloo
significance: Peace/sanctuary town. Burned at the Battle of Tugaloo (August 10, 1776). Permanently destroyed by Williamson. Never reoccupied.

name: Kituwah
significance: Most sacred Cherokee site; the Mother Town where the eternal flame was kept. Approximately 5,000 years of continuous habitation. Platform mound ~170 ft diameter (originally 15–20 ft tall, now ~5 ft due to farming). EBCI purchased 309 acres here in 1996.

name: New Echota
significance: Cherokee national capital 1825–1838. Site of the Cherokee Constitution (1827), the Cherokee Phoenix newspaper (1828–1834), the Cherokee Supreme Court, and the Treaty of New Echota (1835). Purpose-built as a modern capital with a council house, courthouse, print shop, and missionary station.
status: New Echota Historic Site, Georgia State Parks (reconstructed buildings open to the public)

name: Tellassee
significance: Overhill town on the Little Tennessee River near its confluence with the Tellico River. Appeared on Timberlake's 1762 map as one of the principal Overhill settlements.

name: Mialoquo
significance: Home of Dragging Canoe. Destroyed 1776 by Colonel William Christian's Virginia militia. Population followed Dragging Canoe south to establish the Chickamauga towns rather than rebuilding. Never reoccupied.

name: Chestowee
significance: Overhill/Valley settlement near the mouth of Chestuee Creek. Burned by John Sevier in December 1780. Population dispersed south and west. Never rebuilt.

name: Ellijay
significance: Middle town whose name means 'place of green things.' Located on Ellijay Creek, a tributary of the Little Tennessee in Macon County, NC.
status: Rural area near modern Franklin, NC

name: Watauga
significance: Cherokee Middle town on the Little Tennessee River, distinct from the later Euro-American Watauga settlement in northeast Tennessee.
status: Rural area in Macon County, NC

name: Nununyi
significance: Out Town whose name means 'potato place,' on the Oconaluftee River near present-day Cherokee, NC. Referenced by James Mooney in his Cherokee ethnographic work. One of the oldest Cherokee communities in the area.

name: Joree
significance: Middle town on the upper Little Tennessee River near present-day Franklin, NC. Noted in 18th-century colonial records.

name: Tessuntee
significance: Small Middle town on Tessentee Creek in Macon County, NC. The creek still bears a variant of the Cherokee name.
status: Rural area along Tessentee Creek, Macon County, NC

name: Burning Town
significance: Middle town on Burningtown Creek west of Franklin, NC. Burningtown Creek preserves the name.
status: Rural Burningtown community in Macon County, NC

name: Stickoyi
significance: Small Middle settlement near the Tuckasegee River headwaters in Jackson County, NC.
status: Rural area in Jackson County, NC

name: Seneca
significance: Major Lower town at the confluence of Seneca Creek and the Keowee River. Site of the Battle of Twelve Mile Creek (August 1, 1776). Permanently destroyed by Williamson. Never reoccupied.
status: Modern town of Seneca, SC preserves the name; original site partly under Lake Keowee

name: Toxaway
significance: Lower town near the headwaters of the Toxaway River. Burned 1760 by Montgomery, resettled by 1762. Permanently destroyed 1776 by Williamson. Never reoccupied.

name: Jore
significance: Lower town on Jocassee Creek. Permanently destroyed 1776 by Williamson. Never reoccupied. Lake Jocassee now covers the site.

name: Coneross
significance: Lower town on Coneross Creek. Permanently destroyed 1776 by Williamson. Never reoccupied. Coneross Creek preserves the name.
status: Rural area in Oconee County, SC; Coneross Creek preserves the name

name: Oconaluftee
significance: Principal Out Town on the Oconaluftee River. Became the core of the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians after removal.
status: Within the Qualla Boundary (EBCI reservation); near modern Cherokee, NC

name: Soco
significance: Out Town near Soco Creek and Soco Gap. Located along a major trail connecting the Oconaluftee and Pigeon River valleys.
status: Near Soco Gap on the Blue Ridge Parkway; within Qualla Boundary

name: Qualla
significance: Out Town that gave its name to the Qualla Boundary, the present-day Eastern Band Cherokee reservation.
status: Heart of the modern Qualla Boundary; Cherokee, NC

name: Stecoe
significance: Out Town in Graham County, NC. Situated along Stecoah Creek, a tributary of the Little Tennessee. The Stecoah Valley preserves the name.

name: Tuckasegee
significance: Out Town on the Tuckasegee River in Jackson County, NC. The river takes its name from this Cherokee settlement.
status: Near modern Tuckasegee community in Jackson County, NC

name: Great Hiwassee
significance: Principal Valley town and the largest settlement on the Hiwassee River. Name means 'a savanna' or 'meadow.' Served as a major center of Valley Cherokee life.

name: Quanassee
significance: Valley town on the Hiwassee River downstream from Great Hiwassee. One of the principal Valley settlements.

name: Chestuee
significance: Valley town on Chestuee Creek near its confluence with the Hiwassee River. The name relates to 'rabbit place.'
status: Rural area near Benton, TN; Chestuee Creek preserves the name

name: Nottely
significance: Valley town on the Nottely River. The Nottely River and Lake Nottely preserve the Cherokee toponym.

name: Amoyee
significance: Valley town on the Hiwassee River in Cherokee County, NC. Referenced in Mooney's ethnographic survey.

name: Peachtree
significance: Valley town at the confluence of Peachtree Creek and the Hiwassee River. The Peachtree Mound archaeological site nearby shows long Mississippian-era occupation.
status: Near modern Murphy, NC; Peachtree Mound is a documented archaeological site

name: Hanging Dog
significance: Valley town on Hanging Dog Creek. One of the last Cherokee settlements in the region before removal.
status: Rural community northwest of Murphy, NC; Hanging Dog Creek preserves the name

name: Conasauga
significance: Valley town on the Conasauga River near the TN-GA border. The river preserves the Cherokee name and is home to exceptionally high aquatic biodiversity.
status: Rural area along the Conasauga River

name: Etowah (Hightower)
significance: Major Cherokee town at the confluence of the Etowah and Oostanaula rivers. Capital of the Etowah judicial district, one of the eight Cherokee National Council districts. Destroyed by John Sevier in 1782, rebuilt. Attacked again in 1793 at the Battle of Hightower; war chief Kingfisher killed. Rebuilt again and survived to removal.
status: Near present-day Rome, GA; site largely built over

name: Nacoochee
significance: Cherokee settlement in the Nacoochee Valley with a large Mississippian-era platform mound showing thousands of years of habitation. The valley was one of the most fertile farming areas in the Cherokee Nation. After removal, white settlers built a gazebo on top of the mound.
status: Nacoochee Mound survives with a gazebo built on it in the 1800s; visible from GA Highway 17

name: Coosawattee
significance: Valley town on the Coosawattee River in present-day Gilmer County, GA. Grew in importance as Cherokee settlements shifted southward in the late 18th century.
status: Submerged under Carters Lake (U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, 1977)

name: Running Water
significance: Five Lower Towns refuge of Dragging Canoe; major Chickamauga base 1782–1794
status: Submerged under Nickajack Lake near Whiteside, TN

name: Nickajack
significance: Five Lower Towns refuge; destroyed by U.S. forces under Major James Ore in September 1794, ending the Chickamauga War

name: Long Island Town
significance: Five Lower Towns refuge on the Tennessee River near present Bridgeport, AL
status: Long Island still visible in the river

name: Crow Town
significance: Five Lower Towns refuge in northeast Alabama

name: Lookout Mountain Town
significance: Five Lower Towns refuge at the foot of Lookout Mountain
